claims.text: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni has a single-phase FCC structure.
Equiatomic CrCoNi is a single-phase FCC ternary derivative of Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
All quaternary and ternary alloys in the proposed comparison are single-phase FCC after identical thermomechanical processing.
Mechanical-property differences among the alloys arise from local chemical short-range order rather than constituent count alone.
The greater chemical complexity of the quinary alloy produces more pronounced local chemical short-range order than in the quaternary and ternary alloys.
More pronounced local chemical order increases the effective stacking-fault energy.
Higher stacking-fault energy promotes dislocation cross-slip and dynamic recovery over planar slip and early twin nucleation.
Cross-slip and dynamic recovery distribute strain more uniformly and delay localized deformation.
The proposed dislocation behavior gives the quinary alloy greater work hardening than the lower-component alloys.
The proposed dislocation behavior gives the quinary alloy greater ductility than the lower-component alloys.
Under identical test conditions, the quinary alloy will have higher effective stacking-fault energy than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
Under identical test conditions, the quinary alloy will show more cross-slip and a more uniform dislocation distribution than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
Under identical test conditions, the quinary alloy will show higher work-hardening rate and ductility than the quaternary and ternary alloys.
Holding strain rate, temperature, geometry, surface condition, and thermomechanical history constant isolates compositional complexity as the sole cause of observed differences.
The exact origin of the exceptional mechanical properties of the CrCoNi ternary remains unclear.
The quantitative relationship between local-order magnitude and cross-slip frequency has not been precisely determined.
Partial-dislocation separation measured by high-resolution TEM can be used as a proxy for stacking-fault energy.
In situ synchrotron diffraction can distinguish activation of cross-slip from planar slip in real time.
Failure to observe statistically significant increases in effective stacking-fault energy, cross-slip activity, or distinct local ordering in the quinary alloy would falsify the hypothesis.
